title: THEY THREW GOD’S PROPHET INTO A PIT—BUT THE MAN WHO RISKED EVERYTHING TO SAVE HIM WAS A FOREIGNER
paragraphs: THEY THREW GOD’S PROPHET INTO A PIT—BUT THE MAN WHO RISKED EVERYTHING TO SAVE HIM WAS A FOREIGNER

His name was Ebed-Melech. He wasn't a prophet, a priest, or a celebrated warrior. He was an outsider in a dying kingdom. And when God's own people abandoned Jeremiah to die, this overlooked man did something that exposed the difference between religious appearance and courageous faith.
What if the person God remembers most in a moment of crisis is the one everyone else considers insignificant?
Imagine being trapped in a dark, underground cistern.
No ladder. No food. No way to climb out.
Your feet are sinking into thick mud. Every movement exhausts you. Above your head, the opening grows smaller as daylight fades.
And the people who put you there?
They are not strangers who have never heard of God.
They are leaders of the very nation that claims to belong to Him.
Now imagine hearing footsteps overhead.
Someone has come.
But you don't know whether those footsteps belong to a rescuer—or someone arriving to make sure you never come out.
This was not a fictional nightmare.
This was the suffering of Jeremiah, a prophet of the living God.
And the man who intervened was someone many readers of Scripture have barely noticed.
His name was Ebed-Melech.
He was a Cushite. A foreigner. A royal official.

And his story, recorded in Jeremiah 38:7–13 and continued in Jeremiah 39:15–18, reveals something so powerful about faith, compassion, and God's justice that it deserves to be remembered whenever we are tempted to believe our lives are too small to matter.
Because sometimes the greatest courage in a city does not come from the throne.
Sometimes it comes from the person standing in the shadows who refuses to let another human being die.
Jerusalem was collapsing.

The Babylonian army was tightening its grip around the city. Hunger was spreading. Fear was growing. The political and spiritual leadership of Judah was facing the consequences of years of rebellion against God.
And Jeremiah kept delivering a message nobody wanted to hear.
The city would fall.
Those who remained and resisted Babylon would face death, while those who surrendered would live.
This was not Jeremiah's political preference. It was the word the LORD had given him for that particular moment in Judah's history.
But truth becomes dangerous when powerful people decide that preserving their position matters more than listening to God.
The officials accused Jeremiah of weakening the soldiers and discouraging the people.
They wanted him silenced.
King Zedekiah, who possessed the authority to intervene, surrendered Jeremiah into their hands.
And the officials took the prophet and lowered him into a cistern belonging to Malchiah, a member of the royal household, in the court of the guard.
Jeremiah 38:6 describes what happened.
There was no water in the cistern.
Only mud.
And Jeremiah sank into it.
Pause there.
The man who had faithfully proclaimed God's word was now sinking into a place where he could not save himself.
Faithfulness had not spared him from suffering.
Obedience had not prevented betrayal.
Speaking the truth had not earned him protection from those who should have known better.
Perhaps that is why this story reaches so deeply into the human heart.
Because there are people reading this who know what it feels like to do what is right and still be treated as though they are wrong.
You told the truth, and someone punished you for it.
You tried to protect your family, and your motives were questioned.
You stood for your convictions, and people you trusted walked away.
You prayed. You remained faithful. You tried to honor God.
And somehow, you still ended up in a pit you never expected.

Jeremiah's story does not teach that every painful circumstance is persecution for righteousness. Sometimes we suffer because of our own decisions, sometimes because of other people's sins, and sometimes because we live in a broken world.
But it does show us something important.
Being in a pit does not necessarily mean you have stepped outside God's will.
And being surrounded by religious people does not necessarily mean you are surrounded by people who will act righteously.
Then Scripture introduces a man who changes the direction of the story.
“Now when Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon...” — Jeremiah 38:7, KJV
The Hebrew text introduces him as:
עֶבֶד־מֶלֶךְ הַכּוּשִׁי
ʿEved-Melekh ha-Kushi.
“Ebed-Melech the Cushite.”
The name Ebed-Melech can be understood as “servant of the king,” while ha-Kushi identifies him as a man from Cush, a region associated with lands south of Egypt, particularly ancient Nubia.

The King James Version calls him an Ethiopian, reflecting traditional terminology for that region. But we should not automatically equate the ancient geographical term with the borders of the modern nation of Ethiopia.
The passage also identifies him with the Hebrew word סָרִיס (saris), which can refer to a eunuch or a royal court official. The precise circumstances of his position are not explained.
Scripture does not tell us his age, his family history, or how he entered royal service.
It does tell us what mattered when another man's life was in danger.
He heard.
And he acted.
Ebed-Melech was not one of Judah's celebrated prophets.
He was not presented as a priest responsible for teaching God's law.
He was a foreigner serving inside the royal establishment.
Yet when the leaders of Judah were willing to let God's prophet die, this man recognized the evil of what they had done.
Think about the courage that required.
The officials who condemned Jeremiah were powerful.
The king had already yielded to their demands.
Jerusalem was in crisis.
And Ebed-Melech had every practical reason to remain silent.
He could have told himself that Jeremiah's suffering was none of his business.
He could have protected his position.
He could have waited for someone more influential to speak.
He could have offered a private prayer and walked away.
Instead, he went directly to the king.
Jeremiah 38:9 records his protest:
“My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet...” — KJV
Notice what he did not say.
He did not merely suggest that Jeremiah deserved better treatment.
He did not hide behind cautious political language.
He called the action evil.
In the presence of the king.
Against the conduct of powerful officials.
That is courage.
Not the absence of fear, but the willingness to do what is right despite the cost.
And there is a detail here we must not overlook.
Ebed-Melech did not claim a private revelation. He did not invent a new message from God. He responded to a wrong that was already plainly visible.
A man had been unjustly condemned to die.
And he refused to pretend that silence was righteousness.
There are moments when the most spiritual thing a believer can do is not deliver another speech.
It is to defend someone who is being mistreated.
To tell the truth when deception would be easier.
To protect the vulnerable when indifference would be safer.
To refuse participation in cruelty, even when cruelty has become acceptable to the people around us.
But Ebed-Melech did something else.
Something astonishingly tender.
After the king authorized Jeremiah's rescue, Ebed-Melech gathered men and went to the area beneath the treasury in the royal palace.
There he found old clothes and worn-out rags.
He lowered them into the cistern with ropes.
Why?
Because he was not merely concerned with getting Jeremiah out.
He was concerned with how Jeremiah would be treated while being pulled out.
Listen to his instructions:
“Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords.” — Jeremiah 38:12, KJV
The language is old, but the meaning is beautiful.
Put the worn cloth beneath your arms, Jeremiah.
Place it between your body and the ropes.
Let it cushion you as we lift you.
Can you picture that?
A weakened prophet, trapped in mud.
A rope descending through the darkness.
And with that rope, pieces of old fabric.
Not royal garments.
Not expensive materials.
Just discarded cloth that someone had taken the time to gather.
Ebed-Melech understood that rescuing someone is not only about removing them from danger.
It is also about treating them with dignity.
He cared enough to save Jeremiah's life—and enough to protect his wounded body in the process.
How many people have been helped in ways that left them feeling humiliated?
How many have received assistance wrapped in contempt?
How many have heard the words “I'm only trying to help you” from someone who seemed more interested in proving superiority than showing compassion?
Ebed-Melech offers a different picture.
He did not make Jeremiah's suffering a stage for his own importance.
He did not lecture the prophet from the opening of the cistern.
He did not demand gratitude before lowering the ropes.
He simply prepared what was needed and helped lift the man out.
The Hebrew of Jeremiah 38:13 contains a short, remarkable statement:
וַיַּעֲלוּ אֶת־יִרְמְיָהוּ מִן־הַבּוֹר
Vayyaʿalu et-Yirmeyahu min-habbor.
“And they brought Jeremiah up out of the pit.”
After all the accusations, all the abandonment, all the darkness, and all the mud—
Jeremiah came up.
The prophet who had been lowered into the cistern was lifted out alive.
And the man who initiated that rescue was a foreigner whose faith and courage stood in striking contrast to the conduct of Judah's own leaders.
There is a lesson here that should unsettle every religious heart, including mine.
It is possible to possess religious heritage and still resist God's word.
It is possible to hold authority and still fail to do what is right.
It is possible to be surrounded by sacred language while becoming comfortable with injustice.
And it is possible for someone considered an outsider to demonstrate the trust and obedience that insiders have neglected.
The Bible never teaches that a person's ethnicity determines their standing before God.
The LORD looks beyond the labels human beings use to measure one another.
Ebed-Melech's foreign background did not disqualify him from God's attention.
And the leaders' covenant heritage did not excuse their wrongdoing.
But the story does not end with Jeremiah's rescue.
There is another scene.
One that reveals how closely God had been watching.
In Jeremiah 39, as judgment approaches Jerusalem, the LORD sends Jeremiah a personal message for Ebed-Melech.
Not for the king.
Not for the officials who had condemned the prophet.
For Ebed-Melech.
The man who had gathered old rags.
The man who had spoken up.
The man who had refused to abandon someone in a pit.
God promised to deliver him when disaster came upon the city.
And then came the reason.
“...because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.” — Jeremiah 39:18, KJV
In Hebrew, the closing words include:
כִּי־בָטַחְתָּ בִּי
Ki-vatachta bi.
“Because you trusted in Me.”
Not because Ebed-Melech was politically powerful.
Not because he possessed a prestigious religious title.
Not because he belonged by birth to the nation of Judah.
Because he trusted in the LORD.
That Hebrew verb, batach, communicates trust or reliance.
And the context helps us understand what his trust looked like.
It was not merely a private feeling.
His confidence in God was reflected in the courage to confront wrongdoing and the compassion to preserve a life.
We should be careful here.
The passage does not teach that one courageous act earns salvation or that every faithful believer will be rescued from every physical danger.
God's promise to Ebed-Melech was a specific promise of preservation amid Jerusalem's approaching disaster.
But it reveals something enduring about God's character.
He was not indifferent to this man's trust.
He saw the courage that others might have overlooked.
He knew the heart behind the rescue.
And He spoke a promise into the life of someone who might otherwise have disappeared from history.
Now consider something even more remarkable.
Ebed-Melech was called a servant of the king.
Yet the king he served was frightened, compromised, and unable to save his own kingdom.
Ebed-Melech's true security would not come from the palace.
It would come from the LORD in whom he trusted.
And this is where the story begins to turn our eyes toward Jesus Christ.
We must not force Ebed-Melech into being a direct prophecy of Jesus. Jeremiah 38 is a historical account of a real rescue, not a passage that explicitly identifies Ebed-Melech as a messianic figure.
But when we read this account within the whole testimony of Scripture, we encounter themes that lead us to the heart of the Gospel.
The righteous suffer.
Human authority fails.
The vulnerable need rescue.
And God's mercy reaches people whom others have dismissed.
Jeremiah was rejected for speaking the truth God gave him.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ would also be rejected, condemned by human authorities, and subjected to profound injustice.
Yet there is a crucial difference.
Jeremiah needed another human being to lift him out of the cistern.
Jesus willingly entered suffering to accomplish what no ordinary human rescuer could achieve.
He bore our sins.
He died on the cross.
And He rose again.
The rescue of Jeremiah preserved a prophet's earthly life.
The death and resurrection of Jesus open the way to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life for everyone who believes in Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we are good enough to climb out of every pit ourselves.
Not that we can purchase God's favor through courageous actions.
Not that religious performance can erase our guilt.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, gave Himself for sinners and rose victorious over death.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Ebed-Melech's courage is worth imitating.
But Christ's saving work is what we must trust for redemption.
And if we truly belong to Jesus, His grace should begin transforming the way we treat other people.
The person who has received mercy should become more merciful.
The person who has been forgiven should become more willing to forgive.
The person who has been loved by Christ should not become comfortable watching others suffer.
This does not mean we can solve every tragedy.
It does mean we cannot use our limitations as an excuse to abandon the good that God has placed within our reach.
Maybe your opportunity will not look like a dramatic rescue.
Maybe it will look like standing beside someone whose reputation has been unfairly destroyed.
Maybe it will mean defending a child who cannot defend himself.
Maybe it will mean telling the truth about wrongdoing that others want concealed.
Maybe it will mean bringing a meal to someone who has nothing.
Maybe it will mean listening to a person who has been carrying grief in silence.
Or maybe it will mean admitting that you are the one who needs help.
Because there is another side to this story.
Not everyone reading it is standing above the cistern with a rope.
Some are down inside it.
You may have spent months trying to appear strong.
You smile when people ask how you are doing.
You answer, “I'm fine,” because explaining the truth feels exhausting.
You still attend church. You still encourage others. You still try to pray.
But beneath the surface, something hurts.
Perhaps you have fallen into sin and become afraid to confess it.
Perhaps bitterness has been growing quietly in your heart.
Perhaps you are carrying shame from a decision you cannot undo.
Perhaps you feel spiritually dry and wonder whether God has forgotten you.
Hear this carefully.
Jeremiah's cistern was a literal place, and we should not pretend every personal struggle is identical to his suffering.
But the account can remind us that darkness does not make a person invisible to God.
And the Gospel gives us an even greater assurance.
Jesus did not come to save people who had already made themselves righteous.
He came to call sinners to repentance.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He came to give His life as a ransom for many.
You do not need to disguise your sin before Him.
You need to turn from it and come to Him in faith.
You do not need to manufacture a perfect testimony.
You need the Savior who died and rose again.
You do not need to convince God that you deserve His grace.
Grace, by its very nature, is undeserved.
And perhaps the most important question today is not whether you can identify with Jeremiah or Ebed-Melech.
Perhaps it is whether you have truly entrusted your life to Jesus Christ.
Not merely admired Him.
Not merely quoted Him.
Not merely surrounded yourself with Christian content.
But repented and believed the Gospel.
Because it is possible to know the language of faith without surrendering your heart to the Lord.
And it is possible to spend years near the things of God while resisting the very grace that could transform you.
That is not a reason to despair.
It is a reason to respond while you have the opportunity.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing pride, hidden sin, indifference, bitterness, or spiritual compromise in your life, do not harden your heart.
Confess it to God.
Turn toward Christ.
Receive His forgiveness through faith.
And ask Him to make you the kind of person who not only recognizes suffering but responds with love and truth.
There is something deeply moving about the fact that Ebed-Melech used old, unwanted cloth in Jeremiah's rescue.
Those worn-out rags were not valuable in the eyes of the palace.
But in the hands of a compassionate man, they became part of an act of deliverance.
Do not misunderstand the illustration: human beings are not worthless scraps, and our value does not depend on our usefulness.
We bear the image of God.
But the detail reminds us that ordinary things, placed in service of love, can become extraordinarily meaningful.
A message.
A conversation.
A prayer.
A meal.
An honest word spoken at the right time.
A simple act of mercy.
You may not possess great wealth or public influence.
You may never stand before a crowd.
You may never have your name written in a history book.
But that does not mean your obedience is insignificant.
Ebed-Melech did not need to become Jeremiah to serve God faithfully.
He needed to be faithful where God had placed him.
And so do we.
There is a reason this story matters so much to the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Our message has always been rooted in this truth:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because suffering is imaginary.
But because the grace of Christ can bring forgiveness where there was guilt, repentance where there was rebellion, and a transformed life where sin once ruled.
The Gospel does not merely improve our public image.
It changes our standing before God and begins renewing us from within.
And that truth deserves to be proclaimed beyond the walls of a church building.
It deserves to reach the exhausted believer who is struggling to pray.
The father who wants to lead his family toward Christ but does not know where to begin.
The young person quietly questioning whether God is real.
The Christian who has grown lukewarm and needs to return to the Scriptures.
The wounded soul who has confused the failures of religious people with the character of Jesus.
And the unbeliever who has never clearly heard what Christ accomplished through His death and resurrection.
This is why Gospel Warrior continues sharing Scripture-centered articles, biblical teaching, devotionals, and discipleship resources.
And it is why your participation matters.
Not simply to increase the reach of a page, but because someone among your friends may be facing a struggle you know nothing about.
You may never discover who needed these words.
But you can make them available.
And if this article has brought something personal to the surface, I would genuinely love to hear from you.
You do not have to disclose private details or explain a painful situation publicly.
Even a few words can become the beginning of encouragement, prayer, and meaningful fellowship.
Your story may remind another believer that acts of faithful love still matter.
There may come a day when you need to remember that obedience is not always easy, that suffering is not always evidence of God's displeasure, and that the LORD sees faithfulness others overlook.

We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, Christ is exalted, repentance is not avoided, grace is not cheapened, and people are encouraged to grow in genuine discipleship.
If you are already seeking a meaningful way to support Christian outreach, this may be one way to do so.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from pressure.
“...not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
You do not have to give money to earn His approval.
And you should never neglect essential family responsibilities or appropriate support for your local church because someone online made you feel guilty.
These items are not the reason to follow Christ, and no purchase can deepen God's love for you.
They are simply an additional way for the ministry to express appreciation to those who help sustain its work.
These resources are part of our desire to help people move beyond momentary inspiration into sustained biblical learning, prayer, spiritual maturity, and practical obedience.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of God is not a product.
It is Jesus Christ Himself.
Now return with me, one last time, to that cistern in Jerusalem.
The prophet is still below.
The ropes are being lowered.
The worn cloth is waiting.
The man above has already risked his position by confronting injustice.
And somewhere in that desperate moment, a decision has been made.
Jeremiah will not be abandoned if Ebed-Melech can help it.
The Scripture does not tell us whether the two men ever became close friends.
It does not record a long conversation between them.
It does not tell us whether Jeremiah wept when his feet finally touched solid ground.
We must not invent details the Bible has not given us.
But we know enough.
A man was trapped.
Another man acted.
A prophet was rescued.
And God later declared that the rescuer had trusted in Him.
That is not a small story.
It is a testimony to the God who sees beyond rank, nationality, and reputation, and who calls His people to trust Him in ways that bear the fruit of righteousness.
Who around you might need an Ebed-Melech?
And where in your own life do you need to stop pretending you can rescue yourself and turn more fully toward Jesus?
Do not confuse these two rescues.
Ebed-Melech could help Jeremiah out of a cistern.
Only Christ can save sinners from the judgment their sins deserve.
One rescue points us toward human courage and compassion.
The Gospel announces divine grace through the crucified and risen Savior.
And when that grace truly takes hold of a human heart, it begins producing a different kind of life.
A life that tells the truth.
A life that repents.
A life that extends mercy.
A life that refuses to measure people by their status.
A life that remembers the forgotten.
A life that points beyond itself to Jesus.
May we have the courage of Ebed-Melech when others need help, the humility of Jeremiah when we ourselves need rescuing, and above all, the saving faith that rests in Jesus Christ alone.
Because when the world forgets your name, God has not lost sight of you.
And when your strength is not enough, the risen Christ remains mighty to save.
The world may never remember the hands that lowered the rope, but God remembered the heart that refused to walk away.
